sections.description: Approach to the second-trimester pregnant patient presenting with acute abdominal pain and dyspnea, emphasizing stabilization, targeted history and examination, early risk stratification, and multidisciplinary coordination.
key_points: Assess hemodynamic stability, oxygenation, and pain; dyspnea in pregnancy with massive abdominopelvic masses often reflects mechanical restriction rather than primary cardiopulmonary disease.
Perform careful abdominal and bimanual examination to define mass size, tenderness, mobility, and relationship to the uterus; compare abdominal size to gestational age.
Screen for infection (urinalysis/urine culture) and inflammatory response; interpret leukocytosis and CRP in the context of normal pregnancy-related changes.
Evaluate for anemia and iron deficiency, which are common and may be exacerbated by inflammation/hemorrhage from degenerating or torsed lesions.
Provide pregnancy-safe analgesia and positional measures (eg, semi-orthostatic) to mitigate diaphragmatic compression.

Initiate early multidisciplinary involvement (obstetrics, gynecology, radiology, anesthesia, neonatology; gynecologic oncology as needed) to balance maternal and fetal risks and guide imaging and intervention.

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology and Epidemiology of Leiomyomas and Adnexal Masses in Pregnancy
sections.description: Foundational concepts on how leiomyomas and adnexal lesions behave during pregnancy, why they can mimic each other, and how they impact maternal–fetal physiology.
key_points: Uterine leiomyomas are present in ~0.3–10% of pregnancies; adnexal masses in ~1–6%. Hormonal milieu (estrogen, progesterone) and increased perfusion can enlarge fibroids.

Fibroid growth is non-linear: fastest from first to second trimester, slower thereafter; third trimester and puerperium often show regression. Degeneration (eg, red/cystic) can cause acute pain and low-grade fever.
Pedunculated subserosal leiomyomas may torsion, leak, or infarct, presenting with acute abdomen and inflammatory markers, and can be mistaken for adnexal cysts.
Decidualization of endometriomas in pregnancy can produce mural nodules and vascularity that mimic malignancy on imaging.
Mass effect from very large lesions can produce restrictive ventilatory symptoms and positional dyspnea without intrinsic cardiopulmonary pathology.

CA-125 physiology in pregnancy: typically highest in the first and near-term third trimester and lower in the second trimester; mild elevations occur with benign conditions (endometriosis, adenomyosis, leiomyomas) and are not diagnostic of malignancy.

sections.section_title: Differential Diagnosis of Large Cystic Abdominopelvic Masses in the Second Trimester
sections.description: Structured differential and discriminating features for cystic or mixed masses detected during pregnancy.
key_points: Key considerations include degenerating (cystic) leiomyoma, pedunculated subserosal leiomyoma with torsion, decidualized endometrioma, benign ovarian cysts (serous/mucinous), paraovarian cyst, hydrosalpinx, peritoneal inclusion cyst, ovarian torsion, and less commonly, neoplasia.

Clues favoring uterine origin: continuity with myometrium, 'bridging vessel sign' from uterus on Doppler/MRI, beak/claw sign of myometrial interface, absence of normal ipsilateral ovary adjacent to the mass.

Clues favoring endometrioma/ovarian cyst: ovarian stroma adjacent to lesion, T1 hyperintensity with T2 shading (endometrioma), separate normal uterus without feeding vessels, paraovarian plane of cleavage.
Serum tumor markers have limited specificity in pregnancy; isolated CA-125 elevation is non-diagnostic—serial trends and imaging features carry greater weight.
Clinical context (acute torsion pain, fever from necrosis, obstructive pelvic location) helps prioritize emergent conditions even when imaging is indeterminate.

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Workup and Imaging Algorithm in Pregnancy
sections.description: Evidence-based, pregnancy-safe evaluation pathway integrating ultrasound, Doppler, and non-contrast MRI; judicious use of labs and fetal assessment.
key_points: First-line imaging is transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound with color Doppler to document size, morphology (uni-/multilocular cystic, solid components), vascular pattern, and relationship to uterus/placenta.

Non-contrast MRI (preferably 1.5 T) is indicated when ultrasound is indeterminate or masses are large/multiple/posterior; evaluate T1/T2 signal, fat-suppressed sequences, wall thickness, hemorrhagic or solid components, and continuity with uterine tissue.
Avoid gadolinium during pregnancy unless a compelling maternal indication exists; most pelvic mass assessments can be performed without contrast.
Laboratory evaluation: CBC and iron indices for anemia, inflammatory markers, urine culture for UTI; tumor markers only as adjuncts with awareness of pregnancy-related variation.
Fetal assessment for nonobstetric surgery: document fetal heart rate before and after (and intraoperatively when feasible and gestationally appropriate); coordinate with obstetrics and anesthesia.
CT and ionizing radiation are generally avoided but may be justified for life-threatening maternal indications after risk–benefit assessment.

sections.section_title: Management Strategies During Pregnancy: Expectant Versus Surgical
sections.description: Principles for selecting observation or intervention, optimal timing, surgical approach, and perioperative maternal–fetal considerations.
key_points: Default to expectant management for asymptomatic, uncomplicated masses; intervene when there is torsion, rupture, hemorrhage/infection, intractable pain, progressive respiratory compromise, obstructive anatomy, rapid growth with oncologic concern, or diagnostic uncertainty that alters management.
Second trimester (approximately 14–22 weeks) is generally the safest window for nonobstetric surgery, balancing miscarriage and preterm labor risks.

Approach selection: laparoscopy is feasible for selected smaller, pedunculated, or accessible lesions early in gestation using open (Hasson) entry; very large/multiple/intramural or anatomically complex masses often require laparotomy.

Intraoperative principles: minimize uterine manipulation; prioritize hemostasis; consider myomectomy for pedunculated fibroids with torsion/degeneration; avoid intramural myomectomy when risk to pregnancy outweighs benefit; obtain peritoneal fluid for culture/cytology when indicated.

Anesthesia is generally safe in pregnancy with modern agents; individualized use of tocolysis or progesterone—routine prophylaxis is not universally recommended; coordinate intermittent or continuous fetal monitoring based on gestational age and feasibility.

Perioperative care: antibiotic prophylaxis per protocol and culture-directed therapy for concurrent infections; VTE risk assessment and prophylaxis; monitor uterine activity; correct anemia with iron (IV when needed) and transfusion for symptomatic or severe cases.
Shared decision-making and documented informed consent are essential, emphasizing goals to preserve pregnancy, avoid overtreatment, and address maternal indications.

sections.description: Determining mode and timing of delivery, anticipating intrapartum challenges posed by large fibroids, and postnatal surveillance and counseling.
key_points: Delivery mode is individualized by fibroid number, size, and location relative to the cervix and lower uterine segment; obstructive lesions or prior myomectomy with significant myometrial entry often favor elective cesarean delivery.
Aim for delivery at term when maternal–fetal status permits; schedule earlier if obstetric indications arise. Reuse existing midline incisions when appropriate and prepare for hemorrhage.
Large posterior or isthmic fibroids can impede descent and increase cesarean likelihood; pedunculated myomectomy without deep myometrial entry may not mandate cesarean by itself.
Most fibroids regress postpartum; reassess clinically and by imaging before planning interval surgery. Asymptomatic residual fibroids can often be observed.

Neonatal and maternal outcomes are generally excellent with individualized, multidisciplinary care; counsel on recurrence risk, future pregnancy considerations, interpregnancy interval after cesarean/surgery, and contraception.

Clinical pearls: fibroids can mimic adnexal masses; look for bridging vessels; rely on ultrasound plus non-contrast MRI; document fetal heart rate around nonobstetric surgery; intervene only for clear indications and limit surgery to what is necessary to preserve pregnancy.
